query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) high-entropy alloys, the formation and long-term stability of a coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the selective oxidation of the minor element X (especially when X = Al) in concert with Cr. This preferential oxidation creates an oxide layer whose phase composition is inherently compatible (in terms of thermal expansion and lattice matching) with the underlying metallic matrix, thereby reducing interfacial stresses and the propensity for cracking or spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase metallic solid-solution high-entropy alloy CrFeCoNiX.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by intentionally varying the minor addition X (using Si, Mn, or Al) and subjecting these alloys to controlled oxidation or corrosive environments at temperatures above 900 °C.
generation.conditions: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures >900 °C under conditions where scale growth kinetics and interfacial stresses can be assessed.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructure and phase composition of the oxide scale at the alloy surface; specifically, the formation of a continuous, chemically compatible protective oxide (e.g., alumina-rich layer in the case of Al addition or related silicate scale with Si) that adheres well to the metal substrate.
generation.mechanism: Preferential oxidation of the minor element X (e.g., Al) in combination with Cr leads to the formation of a protective oxide with reduced thermal expansion mismatch and improved chemical inertness. This oxide scale evolves slowly and remains coherent because its composition and structure are dictated by the high configurational entropy of the alloy that promotes uniform cation distribution and tailored oxidation pathways.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with an appropriate minor addition (especially Al) will develop a thin, adherent oxide layer that grows slowly and resists cracking/spallation under high-temperature conditions, whereas alloys with less favorable X substitutions (e.g., Mn or Si, if not forming comparably coherent oxides) will show a higher incidence of oxide scale breakdown.
generation.baseline: A comparable CrFeCoNi alloy lacking the minor addition X or containing an element that does not facilitate the formation of a coherent protective oxide.
generation.boundary: Tested in environments above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres, with observations limited to conditions where scale growth kinetics and adhesion mechanisms are active.
generation.uncertainty: The precise role of each minor element (Si, Mn, Al) in modifying oxidation behavior is uncertain without systematic comparative oxidation studies, and the degree to which lattice matching and thermal expansion mismatch drive the scale stability may vary with subtle compositional differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Si, and Mn, alongside a baseline CrFeCoNi alloy without X. Expose all samples to a controlled oxidation environment at temperatures above 900 °C for a fixed period. Characterize the oxide scale for thickness, phase composition (using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy), adhesion (via thermal cycling and mechanical spallation tests), and the prevalence of cracking.
measurements: Phase composition of the oxide scale
Spallation or cracking frequency from mechanical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with the hypothesized beneficial element (e.g., Al) does not show a significantly more stable, coherent, and slow-growing oxide scale compared to both the baseline and the other X variants, then the proposed mechanism—that preferential oxidation of X combined with Cr leads to reduced interfacial stresses and prevents oxide spallation—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Entropy-stabilized oxides

Abstract: Configurational disorder can be compositionally engineered into mixed oxide by populating a single sublattice with many distinct cations. The formulations promote novel and entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter where metal cations are incorporated in new ways. Here, through rigorous experiments, a simple thermodynamic model, and a five-component oxide formulation, we demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt that entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state. In the latter, cation distributions are proven to be random and homogeneous. The findings validate the hypothesis that deliberate configurational disorder provides an orthogonal strategy to imagine and discover new phases of crystalline matter and untapped opportunities for property engineering. The composition of oxide compounds controls many of their properties and electronic phases. Here, the authors show that entropy and configurational disorder can stabilize new phases of oxides, potentially enabling a better engineering of their properties.
